main.title: Heroes of Might and Magic III
main.subtitle: Heroes, armies and the restoration of Erathia
main.summary: Heroes of Might and Magic III: The Restoration of Erathia (commonly referred to as Heroes of Might and Magic 3, or Heroes 3, or abbreviated HoMM 3) is a turn-based strategy game, developed by Jon Van Caneghem through New World Computing and originally released for Microsoft Windows by The 3DO Company in 1999.

cards.heading: New World Computing returns to Erathia
cards.text: Heroes of Might and Magic III: The Restoration of Erathia (commonly referred to as Heroes of Might and Magic 3, or Heroes 3, or abbreviated HoMM 3) is a turn-based strategy game, developed by Jon Van Caneghem through New World Computing and originally released for Microsoft Windows by The 3DO Company in 1999.

cards.heading: Resources, towns and hexagonal battles
cards.text: Heroes cross the map with armies of mythical creatures, collecting resources and artifacts while contesting mines and towns. A captured mine supplies income each turn; a developed town can turn that income into stronger forces. When armies meet, units fight on a hexagonal battlefield. Heroes III adds larger maps, an underground layer and more victory conditions to this rhythm. Some scenarios centre on finding the Grail, which grants a town lasting advantages. Skills also change a hero's options: Diplomacy may turn a potential battle into an opportunity to recruit the opposing force.

cards.heading: Seven campaigns and multiplayer maps
cards.text:
Heroes III can be played alone through a series of campaigns, as well as cooperatively and competitively through multiplayer maps. 50 skirmish maps were included for this purpose.

The game's story unfolds primarily through a series of seven playable campaigns, all set on the continent of Antagarich. During the campaigns, the story is told from alternating points of view, giving players the opportunity to play as each of the town alignments.

main.title: Metal Slug X
main.subtitle: The second campaign remixed
main.summary: Metal Slug X is SNK's reworking of Metal Slug 2, released for Neo Geo MVS in March 1999.

cards.heading: The second campaign remixed
cards.text: Metal Slug X is SNK's reworking of Metal Slug 2, released for Neo Geo MVS in March 1999. Marco, Tarma, Eri and Fio return to the same broad campaign against Morden and an alien threat, but revised encounters and presentation change the route through it. The game keeps the run-and-gun structure of infantry fighting, found weapons and rideable machines. Its revised engine addresses the earlier release's severe slowdown, making the difference apparent in crowded scenes where the player must keep reading attacks and moving through them.

cards.heading: A familiar place, another threat
cards.text: Changes to enemy placement, weapons and the stages' appearance make knowledge of the previous version useful without guaranteeing that an encounter will unfold in exactly the same way. A familiar stretch can introduce another threat or a different opportunity to collect equipment. The central decisions remain immediate: whether to stay inside a vehicle, use a powerful weapon now or preserve it for the next large enemy. The remix works within that established vocabulary, adjusting what appears and when so the campaign develops another rhythm under the player's hands.

cards.heading: A new version with its own rhythm
cards.text: The detailed character animation and destructible scenery remain central to the spectacle. Prisoners, soldiers and machines react throughout the action, giving a short exchange a comic detail alongside its practical danger. Transformations and the enlarged four-character cast also carry over from Metal Slug 2. The relationship between the releases makes X an unusual sequel-era landmark: its identity comes from revisiting an existing adventure and altering the performance, pacing and encounters enough to give that familiar journey another life in the arcade.

main.title: Pepsiman
main.subtitle: A soft-drink mascot cannot stop running
main.summary: Pepsiman is KID's PlayStation action game, released in Japan on 4 March 1999. The advertising mascot runs automatically through streets, buildings and increasingly improbable emergencies while the player steers him around obstacles. The immediate task is to survive the route, collecting Pepsi cans and reaching people apparently in need of the drink. Its four stages combine an uncomplicated running game with an unusually committed promotional premise. Cars, pedestrians and construction equipment become practical hazards, while even the product's own delivery vehicles can obstruct the hero sent to distribute it.

Its four stages combine an uncomplicated running game with an unusually committed promotional premise. Cars, pedestrians and construction equipment become practical hazards, while even the product's own delivery vehicles can obstruct the hero sent to distribute it.

cards.heading: Read the next obstacle before it arrives
cards.text: Running, dashing and different jumps provide the means of responding to the course. Checkpoints soften repeated mistakes, but each section introduces arrangements that must be recognised quickly. Some passages change the rules by placing Pepsiman on a skateboard or trapping him in a metal bin that reverses the controls. Large objects pursue him at the end of stages, turning the camera and the direction of danger into another variation. The player learns a route through repetition, anticipating the next response before the automatically advancing character reaches the point where it becomes necessary.

cards.heading: An advertisement becomes an unlikely cult game
cards.text: The small budget led to inexpensive live-action interludes featuring Mike Butters watching Pepsiman while consuming Pepsi and snacks. Kotaro Uchikoshi contributed to the game's visual production before becoming better known for his narrative games. Although a North American release was considered, Pepsiman remained a Japanese PlayStation title. Its commercial reception was modest, but its absurd premise later attracted a substantial cult following. The game's appeal comes from the consistency of that absurdity: a straightforward obstacle course is presented with the complete seriousness of a world whose every crisis can be answered by one branded superhero.

main.title: Um Jammer Lammy
main.subtitle: Late for the first concert
main.summary: Um Jammer Lammy is NanaOn-Sha's PlayStation rhythm game, released in Japan on 18 March 1999. Lammy, the nervous guitarist of MilkCan, has fifteen minutes to reach her band's concert, but a succession of absurd emergencies blocks the way. Imagining an object as a guitar helps her find the confidence to respond. Masaya Matsuura's musical design again meets Rodney Alan Greenblat's flat, colourful characters, following their work on PaRappa the Rapper. This time the performance is built around guitar phrases, with each interruption becoming another unlikely stage on the way to the real one.

cards.heading: Late for the first concert
cards.text: Um Jammer Lammy is NanaOn-Sha's PlayStation rhythm game, released in Japan on 18 March 1999. Lammy, the nervous guitarist of MilkCan, has fifteen minutes to reach her band's concert, but a succession of absurd emergencies blocks the way. Imagining an object as a guitar helps her find the confidence to respond. Masaya Matsuura's musical design again meets Rodney Alan Greenblat's flat, colourful characters, following their work on PaRappa the Rapper. This time the performance is built around guitar phrases, with each interruption becoming another unlikely stage on the way to the real one.

cards.heading: Answering with a riff
cards.text: A teacher performs a phrase, then Lammy answers through button presses on a scrolling score. Following the pattern keeps the song moving; well-timed improvisation can earn more points and raise the performance from Good to Cool. At that rank, the teacher leaves and the player can keep developing a personal response, provided the rhythm remains convincing. Poor playing lowers the rank and can end the song. The contest therefore asks for more than mechanical repetition: the printed notes establish a phrase that can become a starting point for another variation.

cards.heading: The sound is part of the toy
cards.text: Unlockable effects change Lammy's guitar with distortion, flanging, reverb and other treatments. Shoulder buttons operate a whammy effect, while some settings respond to analogue control. These sound changes are optional and do not increase the score, leaving room to experiment simply because the result is enjoyable. Completing Lammy's story also opens PaRappa's versions of the songs, and multiplayer extends the call-and-response idea to another person. Regional versions changed one episode's setting, but the journey retains its central joke: a shy character repeatedly discovers that she can play her way through the obstruction in front of her.

main.title: Beetle Adventure Racing!
main.subtitle: Paradigm Entertainment / EA Canada · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Beetle Adventure Racing! is Paradigm Entertainment and EA Canada's Nintendo 64 racing game built around the Volkswagen New Beetle. The cars may share a familiar shape, but the elaborate courses provide much of the variety. Branching routes, shortcuts and hidden crates give the player reasons to explore beyond simply following the most obvious road. A first race can reveal another possibility for the next attempt. Learning the course means gradually discovering how its scenery conceals paths that alter both the journey and the chance of reaching the finish first.

cards.heading: A race with another road around the corner
cards.text: Beetle Adventure Racing! is Paradigm Entertainment and EA Canada's Nintendo 64 racing game built around the Volkswagen New Beetle. The cars may share a familiar shape, but the elaborate courses provide much of the variety. Branching routes, shortcuts and hidden crates give the player reasons to explore beyond simply following the most obvious road. A first race can reveal another possibility for the next attempt. Learning the course means gradually discovering how its scenery conceals paths that alter both the journey and the chance of reaching the finish first.

cards.heading: Crates reward looking away from the racing line
cards.text: Championship progress opens vehicles and tracks, while crates placed around the courses encourage finding less direct routes. A useful detour must be weighed against the time it costs, making exploration part of improving a run rather than a completely separate activity. The cars' handling gives the player a familiar point of reference as the surroundings become more elaborate. A cave, jump or gap in the scenery may lead somewhere worth remembering, turning the next lap into a chance to test the route noticed on the last.

cards.heading: The battle continues off the track
cards.text: Two players can race on unlocked courses, while Beetle Battle allows up to four competitors to collect coloured ladybugs, attack one another and escape once the set is complete. That mode turns the vehicles toward a different kind of route-finding contest. The Australian edition replaced the Volkswagens with Holden models and used the name HSV Adventure Racing. Released in 1999, the game remains distinctive for making a small car selection support unusually exploratory tracks, allowing discovery itself to become one of the skills behind a faster race.

main.title: Blue Stinger
main.subtitle: Stranded on Dinosaur Island
main.summary: Blue Stinger is Climax Graphics' action adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 25 March 1999.

cards.heading: Stranded on Dinosaur Island
cards.text: Blue Stinger is Climax Graphics' action adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 25 March 1999. Emergency rescuer Eliot Ballade becomes stranded on Dinosaur Island, where monsters have overrun the complex. Working with other survivors and the mysterious Nephilim, he searches for a way through the island and the cause of the disaster. Exploration opens new areas through found items, while a variety of weapons supports the fighting. Producer Shinya Nishigaki conceived the project as a tribute to Western action films, giving its strange crisis the shape of an escalating rescue adventure.

cards.heading: Supplies inside the disaster
cards.text: The player can control Eliot or Dogs Bower while exploring the island's three-dimensional environments. Weapons and other supplies can be found or purchased, connecting combat to the resources gathered along the route. Optional missions offer further equipment, giving a detour a practical reward before the next dangerous area. Moving through the complex requires both defeating its inhabitants and finding the items that open another section. The relationship between shopping, exploration and fighting gives the disaster an unusual everyday detail: supplies remain useful commodities even while the surrounding island has become hostile.

cards.heading: A changing view of the action
cards.text: The Japanese edition uses fixed camera positions, while the Western version follows behind the character and adds an optional first-person view. The change affects how the player reads the same spaces and approaches their threats. Monster designer Robert Short and storyboard artist Pete von Sholly were among the American contributors, while Toshihiko Sahashi composed the music. Blue Stinger accompanied Dreamcast's Western launch, presenting the new machine through a substantial three-dimensional adventure. Its mixture of colourful supplies, grotesque creatures and cinematic staging gave that early showcase a personality of its own.

main.title: Pokémon Pinball
main.subtitle: Jupiter / HAL Laboratory · Game Boy Color
main.summary: Pokémon Pinball is Jupiter and HAL Laboratory's Game Boy Color pinball game, turning the series' collecting journey into play across two themed tables. The ball is a Poké Ball, while familiar creatures supply bumpers and other features around the board. Points remain the immediate reward for keeping it moving, but encounters also build a Pokédex containing the original 151 Pokémon. The collection is preserved between games, making a successful session useful even when the ball eventually escapes the flippers and the current score can no longer grow.

cards.heading: The Poké Ball becomes an actual ball
cards.text: Pokémon Pinball is Jupiter and HAL Laboratory's Game Boy Color pinball game, turning the series' collecting journey into play across two themed tables. The ball is a Poké Ball, while familiar creatures supply bumpers and other features around the board. Points remain the immediate reward for keeping it moving, but encounters also build a Pokédex containing the original 151 Pokémon. The collection is preserved between games, making a successful session useful even when the ball eventually escapes the flippers and the current score can no longer grow.

cards.heading: Complete the encounter before time runs out
cards.text: Red and Blue tables have different layouts and ways to reach their special modes. In Catch Mode, repeated bumper hits reveal a Pokémon's image before the creature appears on the table as the next target. Further hits complete the capture. Changing location alters which Pokémon can be encountered, connecting the route through table features with progress in the larger collection. The player is learning the angles of a pinball game while also looking for another useful meeting within the familiar Pokémon world.

cards.heading: The cartridge pushes back
cards.text: A built-in rumble feature gives the cartridge an unusual enlarged shape and provides physical feedback while the ball rebounds around the table. The Game Boy Color's screen supplies a bright setting for the two boards, while the game's saved Pokédex gives them a shared long-term purpose. Released in 1999, Pokémon Pinball made an especially direct connection between the licence and a different genre: the object used to catch a Pokémon becomes the object controlled throughout the game, joining a small sporting action to the continuing pleasure of collecting.

main.title: Omega Boost
main.subtitle: Polyphony leaves the road for open space
main.summary: Omega Boost is Polyphony Digital's PlayStation shooting game, first released in Japan on 22 April 1999. The player controls a flying mecha through waves of enemies, using movement and target selection to survive a rapid sequence of combat situations. Mechanical designs by Shōji Kawamori give the central machine a recognisable character. It is an unusual work from a studio associated with Gran Turismo, turning its attention from racing cars to a science-fiction action spectacle. The immediate task is to understand the surrounding formation quickly enough to remove its threats before they close in.

The player controls a flying mecha through waves of enemies, using movement and target selection to survive a rapid sequence of combat situations. Mechanical designs by Shōji Kawamori give the central machine a recognisable character. It is an unusual work from a studio associated with Gran Turismo, turning its attention from racing cars to a science-fiction action spectacle. The immediate task is to understand the surrounding formation quickly enough to remove its threats before they close in.

cards.heading: Choose within the incoming wave
cards.text: Enemy groups arrive in a fixed sequence, allowing the player to learn their patterns, but the order of targets within each wave remains a choice. Movement offers room to adjust position and bring another opponent into the attack. Some stages allow greater freedom while others constrain speed or direction, changing the conditions without abandoning the central control of the machine. Repeated attempts reveal how a formation is assembled. The player can then act earlier, turning a first impression of visual chaos into a more deliberate sequence of targets and evasive movements.

cards.heading: A short detour with a distinct machine
cards.text: Yasushi Taki and Zaika Tei directed the project, with Kazunori Yamauchi producing and Jun Kitagawa composing the music. The main campaign contains nine stages and additional unlockable special missions. Some reviewers found that scope too brief or the action too simple, while the presentation showed another use for the studio's technical experience. International releases arrived in September 1999. Omega Boost remains Polyphony's singular departure from racing, making it a useful glimpse of how the team approached speed and motion when the vehicle could move through three-dimensional space instead of following a road.

main.title: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike
main.summary: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike - Fight for the Future is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.text: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike - Fight for the Future is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the second and final updated version of Street Fighter III, following Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact. Like its predecessors, it runs on the CP System III hardware.

3rd Strike increased the character roster by adding five new characters, notably including Chun-Li. It also added further refinements to the previous game's play mechanics and rules, including improvements to the parry system. It was ported to the Dreamcast in 2000. In 2004, it was released on the PlayStation 2 and Xbox as part of the Street Fighter Anniversary Collection. A downloadable online version titled Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike Online Edition was released on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2011.

Although not very popular upon release, it amassed positive reviews, and eventually gained a large cult following years after release. The game has a significant competitive gaming scene, which included Evo Moment 37 (also known as the "Daigo Parry"), often considered the most iconic moment in competitive gaming history. On May 29, 2018, Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike was released as a part of the Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One.

main.title: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere
main.subtitle: Air combat enters an imagined future
main.summary: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere is Namco's PlayStation aerial combat game, first released in Japan on 27 May 1999. Fighter missions move into a futuristic world, giving the series a science-fiction setting beyond its earlier contemporary aircraft conflicts. Players still pursue enemy formations and complete objectives from the cockpit, but the Japanese release places those sorties within a branching story. Decisions and relationships affect the route through the campaign. The result gives the next mission a narrative consequence alongside the immediate task of surviving it and bringing down the designated targets.

cards.heading: Air combat enters an imagined future
cards.text: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere is Namco's PlayStation aerial combat game, first released in Japan on 27 May 1999. Fighter missions move into a futuristic world, giving the series a science-fiction setting beyond its earlier contemporary aircraft conflicts. Players still pursue enemy formations and complete objectives from the cockpit, but the Japanese release places those sorties within a branching story. Decisions and relationships affect the route through the campaign. The result gives the next mission a narrative consequence alongside the immediate task of surviving it and bringing down the designated targets.

cards.heading: The campaign can take another route
cards.text: The Japanese edition spans two discs and uses its story to connect the player's choices to different missions and outcomes. Characters and rival interests become part of deciding where the pilot goes next. The aircraft and landscapes support that future setting, while the basic action remains accessible air combat rather than a strict simulation. Takuya Iwasaki and Atsushi Shiozawa directed the project, with a writing contribution from Dai Satō. Its ambition lies in making a flight campaign a story with alternatives rather than a single unchanging list of operations.

cards.heading: Two very different Electrospheres
cards.text: Financial constraints led to a substantially reduced international version, released in Europe and North America in 2000. The branching Japanese story and much of its presentation were removed, changing how the same combat was experienced. This difference helps explain the game's uneven reception across regions. The Japanese edition has since attracted renewed attention for its narrative ambition and unusual place within Ace Combat. Its electronic score, by a team including Tetsukazu Nakanishi, Hiroshi Okubo and Go Shiina, further separates this imagined future from the series' more familiar military settings.
